observations: body L10: the Arabic words are printed so; the shadda of «الظنّ» stands over the nun.
body L14-L15: the Arabic words «ظهر لبعضهم» («visum est quibusdam») are divided between the lines, the opening parenthesis at the end of L14 and the closing one after «لبعضهم» at the head of L15.
body L15: «(١٢٨٥)» is printed in Arabic-Indic numerals.
body L20: the last Arabic word is printed «مُسلا», with a damma over its first letter; Nallino's «utpote iure recepta» renders مُسَلَّمًا, «granted», which has a second mim; kept as printed.
body L2, L5: a speck stands under the v of «intervallo» and another over the u of «deminutionis»; they are not signs.
notes_right L4: the closing bracket after «24°» is printed broken, like a vertical stroke.
notes_left L5-L6: the name of Qāḍī-zādeh is divided between the lines, a hyphen at the end of L5 and a longer dash at the head of L6.

notes_right L8-L11: Nallino's addenda et emendanda in Part II (pp. XXI-XXII; AB01-PDF0438-body-L020 to AB01-PDF0439-body-L019) trace what is told in this note of Euclid and the obliquity of the ecliptic to Heron of Alexandria's commentary on Euclid. An-Nayrīzī (on IV, 16, in Gerard of Cremona's version, ed. Curtze, p. 152) quotes Heron: Euclid set the figure of the sixteenth proposition of book IV because the arc between the equinoctial and either solstitial circle receives the figure of fifteen equal sides (the Latin has twelve, which Nallino marks sic). Proclus Diadochus, on the eighth proposition of Euclid's first book (ed. Friedlein, pp. 268-269), defending the seventh, says the like: the last problem of book IV, the side of the fifteen-sided polygon inscribed in a circle, serves astronomy, since the poles of the equinoctial and of the zodiac stand apart by that side. The comparison is old: Theon of Smyrna (ed. Hiller, pp. 199 and 203; ed. Martin, pp. 324 and 334), after Eudemus, gives the distance between the axis of the fixed stars and the axis of the planets as the side of the fifteen-sided polygon, 24°.
